analysis.one_liner: Closes a banking charter loophole that lets commercial companies own banks without normal federal oversight.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill on a narrow 28-25 vote in June 2022, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Industrial loan companies (ILCs) are state-chartered lenders that can take deposits and make loans like a bank, but the law exempts them from the rule that a company owning a bank must submit to oversight by the Federal Reserve. That exemption has let retail and technology companies own insured banks without the consolidated supervision applied to other bank owners. This bill would close that door going forward: no new ILC would get federal deposit insurance after a September 2021 cutoff (companies with applications already pending could still be approved, but only by a two-thirds vote of the FDIC board after a public hearing, and only within two years). Parent companies of existing ILCs would face the same Federal Reserve reporting and examination requirements as bank holding companies, sales of control of an ILC would generally need to be approved, and the Government Accountability Office would study the effect of ILCs on the economy.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and banking customers gain a system in which commercial conglomerates cannot own FDIC-insured banks while dodging the Federal Reserve supervision that applies to every other bank owner — reducing the risk that a parent company's troubles drain its bank, and limiting the mixing of banking with commerce. Traditional banks gain because new charter-based competitors are cut off.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors, bank customers, and traditional banks

how_it_helps.text: It would bar FDIC deposit insurance for any new industrial loan company approved after September 23, 2021, stopping new commercial companies from using the charter to escape bank holding company rules.
It would give the Federal Reserve the same authority to examine and require reports from ILC parent companies that it has over bank holding companies, closing the main oversight gap.
It would generally require regulators to disapprove changes in control of an ILC, with narrow exceptions, preventing companies from buying their way into the charter.
It would require the Government Accountability Office to study and report to Congress within a year on how ILCs affect competition, market structure, and different industries.

analysis.who_pays: Technology, retail, and lending companies that want to own an insured bank through the ILC charter would be shut out after September 2021. Existing ILC parent companies would bear new Federal Reserve examination and reporting costs even as they keep their exemption.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fintech firms and commercial companies seeking bank charters

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers every industrial loan company in existence, and every application already pending, as of September 23, 2021 — so the companies already using the loophole would have kept it permanently, and the restriction would apply only to future entrants.

Pending applications were not killed outright: the FDIC could still approve them with a two-thirds board vote and a public comment period, and any application not approved by September 23, 2023 would be deemed denied — leaving a defined window for new exceptions.

Opponents of closing the loophole argue that ILC charters let retailers, payments companies, and lenders offer banking-style services without the full cost of holding-company regulation, and that shutting the door to new charters reduces competition and lending options for consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real regulatory gap: companies that mix banking with commerce could own insured banks while escaping the consolidated oversight that applies to other bank owners, and the GAO study would have given Congress a factual record on the consequences. But the design was half-measure by its own terms: it permanently grandfathered every existing ILC and let pending applications through with only a slower process, so the loophole would have stayed largely intact for the institutions already using it. Consumer advocates would call it a necessary first step; fintech interests would call it a protectionist wall raised by incumbent banks, and some new entrants shut out by the date cutoff might have offered borrowers genuine alternatives. On balance it modestly favored financial stability over expansion, at the cost of freezing in place the very companies it was aimed at.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it 28-25 in June 2022, but House leadership never scheduled a vote by the full House before the term ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia introduced the bill on November 9, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On June 22, 2022, the committee held a markup session and voted 28-25 to order the bill reported to the House, in an amended substitute form.
No further action followed: the bill was never debated or voted on by the full House, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Technology, retail, and commercial companies kept the ILC loophole open, and existing industrial loan companies kept their exemption from bank holding company rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tech firms and existing ILCs kept the loophole

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew bipartisan sponsorship (the Democratic sponsor plus 2 Republican and 1 Democratic cosponsors) and cleared committee by a narrow 28-25 vote, but the sources do not give the party breakdown of that vote, and the House never held a floor vote.

industries.industry: Fintech and technology companies seeking ILC charters
industries.note: The bill's September 2021 cutoff would have shut new entrants out of the ILC charter, blocking the path that payments and lending companies have used to offer banking services without Federal Reserve supervision of their parent firms. Consumers would face fewer tech-run banking options but a tighter-overshight system.

industries.industry: Existing industrial loan companies and their parent companies
industries.note: Every ILC existing or applied-for before September 2021 would be permanently exempt from the bank holding company definition — locked into its lighter-touch regulatory treatment — though their parent companies would gain new Federal Reserve reporting and examination requirements.

industries.industry: Traditional banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: Banks compete with ILCs and their corporate owners, and closing the charter to new entrants protects that market position. Here the banks' competitive interest runs alongside the prudential argument for closing the loophole, though it also means less pressure from new competitors.

industries.industry: Retailers and commercial firms that own insured depositories through ILCs
industries.note: Existing commercial owners would keep their charters but, for those approved after the cutoff, face examination authority and possible restrictions on transactions with their bank subsidiaries. The bill is designed to stop the next Walmart-style charter, not unwind the current ones.
